requirements: The core contributions of 'SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models' have been reproduced, including the per-channel smoothing transformation that migrates quantization difficulty from activations to weights, the O1-O3 W8A8 quantization settings, accuracy-preserving INT8 quantization across OPT/BLOOM/GLM/MT-NLG/LLaMA/Llama-2/Falcon/Mistral/Mixtral models, and the measured speedup and memory savings in PyTorch and FasterTransformer.

sub_tasks.requirements: The quantization primitives and granularity definitions from Section 2 have been implemented, including INT8 uniform symmetric quantization (Equation 1), static vs dynamic quantization, and per-tensor, per-token, and per-channel/group-wise granularity with outer-dimension scaling for INT8 GEMM (Equation 2, Figure 3).

The INT8 uniform symmetric quantization function has been implemented per Equation 1: X̄^INT8 = round(X^FP16 / Δ), where Δ = max(|X|) / (2^(N-1) - 1) with N=8, assuming the tensor is symmetric around 0.
The quantization step size Δ has been implemented per Equation 1 as Δ = max(|X|) / (2^(N-1) - 1), computing the maximum absolute value of the tensor X and dividing by (2^(N-1) - 1).
The rounding operator ⌈·⌋ from Equation 1 has been implemented, applying round-to-nearest-integer to X^FP16 / Δ to produce the quantized INT8 tensor X̄^INT8.

The quantization implementation assumes the tensor is symmetric around 0 (no zero-point offset), as stated in Section 2's description of Equation 1: 'we assume the tensor is symmetric at 0 for simplicity'; this symmetric quantization scheme (without an added zero-point) has been used for the primary INT8 quantization implementation.

The bit-width parameter N has been set to 8 in the quantization function of Equation 1, so that the quantization range 2^(N-1) - 1 evaluates to 127, matching the paper's stated use of INT8 (specifically 8-bit) quantization throughout the method.

Static quantization has been implemented, where the quantization step size Δ is pre-computed offline using activation statistics gathered from calibration samples drawn from the pre-training dataset, as described in Section 2.
Dynamic quantization has been implemented, where the quantization step size Δ is computed at runtime from the actual activation statistics of each input, as described in Section 2.
Per-tensor quantization has been implemented, using a single quantization step size Δ for the entire activation or weight matrix, as illustrated in Figure 3 and described in Section 2.

Per-token quantization has been implemented for activations, using a different quantization step size for each token (i.e., each row along the T dimension of X), as illustrated in Figure 3 and described in Section 2.

Per-channel quantization has been implemented for weights, using a different quantization step size for each output channel (C_o dimension of W), as illustrated in Figure 3 and described in Section 2.

Group-wise quantization has been implemented as a coarser-grained version of per-channel quantization, using a shared quantization step size for groups of channels rather than every individual channel, as described in Section 2 citing Shen et al. (2020) and Yao et al. (2022).

The outer-dimension rescaling formulation from Equation 2 has been implemented: Y = diag(Δ_X^FP16) · (X̄^INT8 · W̄^INT8) · diag(Δ_W^FP16), where per-token/per-channel scaling factors are applied only along the outer dimensions (T for activations, C_o for weights) after the INT8 GEMM completes, consistent with hardware constraints for Tensor Core MMA execution described in Section 3.

The core INT8 GEMM computation X̄^INT8 · W̄^INT8 has been implemented such that the matrix multiplication executes entirely in INT8 integer arithmetic (producing an INT32 accumulator internally), with no floating-point rescaling performed inside the GEMM kernel itself, consistent with Section 3's statement that scaling can only be applied after the matrix multiplication finishes because hardware-accelerated GEMM kernels (e.g., Tensor Core MMAs) do not tolerate the insertion of lower-throughput instructions like conversions or CUDA Core FMAs mid-sequence.

The activation-side rescaling diag(Δ_X^FP16) from Equation 2 has been implemented such that the FP16 quantization step size(s) for activations are applied only along the outer T (token) dimension of the INT8 GEMM output, i.e. a single scalar or one scale-per-token is multiplied into each row of the INT32/INT8 GEMM result, rather than being applied per-element or per-input-channel inside the GEMM.

The weight-side rescaling diag(Δ_W^FP16) from Equation 2 has been implemented such that the FP16 quantization step size(s) for weights are applied only along the outer C_o (output channel) dimension of the INT8 GEMM output, i.e. a single scalar or one scale-per-output-channel is multiplied into each column of the INT32/INT8 GEMM result, rather than being applied per-element or per-output-row inside the GEMM.

A verification test has been implemented and run confirming that the full composed dequantization Y = diag(Δ_X^FP16) · (X̄^INT8 · W̄^INT8) · diag(Δ_W^FP16) from Equation 2 produces a floating-point output Y that closely approximates the original FP16 matrix multiplication result X·W (within quantization error tolerance), verifying the correctness of the outer-dimension rescaling composition after the INT8 GEMM completes.

The implementation reflects the hardware rationale from Section 3 that scaling can only be performed along the outer dimensions of the matrix multiplication because hardware-accelerated GEMM kernels rely on a sequence of high-throughput operations (e.g., Tensor Core MMAs) that do not tolerate insertion of lower-throughput instructions (e.g., conversions or CUDA Core FMAs) mid-sequence; the rescaling code must therefore be implemented as a post-GEMM epilogue operation rather than fused into the per-element GEMM inner loop.

The implementation enforces that activation scaling factors Δ_X vary at most per-token (one value per row along T) and weight scaling factors Δ_W vary at most per-output-channel (one value per column along C_o), and explicitly does NOT support arbitrary per-element or true per-input-channel (i.e., along C_i, the reduction dimension) scaling within the GEMM, consistent with Section 3's explanation of why per-channel activation quantization (which would require scaling along the reduction dimension C_i) is infeasible for standard INT8 GEMM kernels and motivates the SmoothQuant smoothing approach instead.

The linear-layer notation from Section 2 (Y = X·W with Y ∈ R^{T×C_o}, X ∈ R^{T×C_i}, W ∈ R^{C_i×C_o}, where T is number of tokens, C_i is input channel count, C_o is output channel count, batch dimension omitted for simplicity) has been implemented consistently across the codebase's quantized linear-layer modules, matching Figure 3's depicted tensor shapes.

The implementation reflects Section 2's rationale that W8A8 quantization (quantizing both weights and activations to INT8, not just weights) is required to utilize integer GEMM kernels (e.g., INT8 GEMM) supported by a wide range of hardware (NVIDIA GPUs, Intel CPUs, Qualcomm DSPs), as opposed to weight-only INT8 quantization which only reduces storage by half without accelerating compute.

The review of quantization difficulty from Section 3 has been reproduced, including the activation outlier visualization (Figure 4) and the Table 1 comparison of per-tensor, per-token, and per-channel activation quantization schemes on OPT models.

The activation and weight magnitude visualization from Figure 4 (left) has been reproduced for a linear layer exhibiting large quantization error, plotting input activation X and weight W magnitudes across the token and channel dimensions to visually contrast their distributions.

The reproduced Figure 4 (left) visualization demonstrates that the weight distribution of the linear layer is quite uniform and flat, making it easy to quantize, consistent with the observation in Section 3 point 1 that quantizing LLM weights with INT8 does not degrade accuracy.

The reproduced activation visualization from Figure 4 (left) shows that outlier activation values are approximately 100x larger in magnitude than most other activation values, consistent with the claim in Section 3 point 2.

The reproduced activation visualization from Figure 4 (red-highlighted channels) demonstrates that outliers appear in a small fraction of fixed channels and persist across all tokens, i.e., high variance across channels for a given token but low variance across tokens for a given outlier channel, consistent with Section 3 point 3.

The SmoothQuant smoothing transformation from Section 4 has been implemented, including the per-channel smoothing factor with migration strength alpha (Equations 3-4), fusion of the factor into previous layers offline, and application to Transformer blocks with the precision mapping in Figure 6.

The per-channel smoothing factor vector s ∈ R^{C_i} has been implemented per Equation 3-4 of Section 4, defined per input channel j (j=1,...,C_i) of the activation X, used to divide activations and multiply weights to keep the linear layer mathematically equivalent.

The mathematically equivalent smoothing transformation from Equation 3 has been implemented: Y = (X·diag(s)^-1)·(diag(s)·W) = X̂·Ŵ, where the smoothed activation X̂ and adjusted weight Ŵ are computed and combined to reproduce the original linear layer output Y before quantization. The smoothed activation X̂ = X·diag(s)^-1 has been implemented, dividing each input channel j of the activation tensor X by the corresponding per-channel smoothing factor s_j, as specified in Equation 3 of Section 4.

A reproduction-side numerical verification test has been implemented and executed confirming that computing Y = X̂·Ŵ (using the smoothed activation and adjusted weight) produces results numerically equivalent, within floating-point tolerance, to computing Y = X·W directly on the original unscaled tensors, thereby validating the mathematical equivalence claimed in Section 4's text following Equation 3. The migration strength hyperparameter α has been implemented in the smoothing factor formula from Equation 4: s_j = max(|X_j|)^α / max(|W_j|)^(1-α), controlling how much quantization difficulty is migrated from activations to weights, with X_j and W_j indexed consistently by the same input channel j.

The activation-side term of the smoothing factor formula from Equation 4, max(|X_j|)^α, has been implemented such that the per-input-channel maximum absolute activation value max(|X_j|) is computed for each input channel j and raised to the power α, where α is the migration strength hyperparameter.

The weight-side term of the smoothing factor formula from Equation 4, max(|W_j|)^(1-α), has been implemented such that the per-input-channel maximum absolute weight value max(|W_j|) is computed for each input channel j (aggregated across all output channels for that input channel) and raised to the power (1-α).

The full Equation 4 smoothing factor s_j = max(|X_j|)^α / max(|W_j|)^(1-α) has been implemented by dividing the activation-side term by the weight-side term independently for each input channel j, producing the per-channel smoothing factor vector s used in Equation 3, with X_j and W_j indexed consistently by the same input channel j across both tensors.

The implementation of Equation 4 correctly reflects that increasing α shifts more of the quantization difficulty from activations to weights (since a higher exponent on max(|X_j|) combined with a lower exponent on max(|W_j|) makes s_j larger, shrinking the smoothed activation X̂ and enlarging the adjusted weight Ŵ), and decreasing α shifts difficulty in the opposite direction, consistent with the description in Section 4 of α as the 'migration strength' controlling how much of the quantization difficulty is migrated from activations to weights.

The Equation 4 smoothing factor implementation correctly handles the boundary cases α=0 (s_j = 1/max(|W_j|), migrating no difficulty to weights from the activation side, i.e. s_j depends only on weights) and α=1 (s_j = max(|X_j|), migrating all activation outlier magnitude into the weights), verifying the formula degenerates sensibly at the extremes of the [0,1] range for the migration strength hyperparameter.

A reproduction-side verification test has been implemented and executed confirming that, using the smoothing factor s_j computed via the Equation 4 formula max(|X_j|)^α / max(|W_j|)^(1-α) for a given α, the resulting smoothed activation X̂ = X·diag(s)^-1 and adjusted weight Ŵ = diag(s)·W satisfy X̂·Ŵ ≈ X·W within floating-point tolerance, thereby confirming that the specific Equation 4 parameterization of s preserves the mathematical equivalence described conceptually in Section 4's text following Equation 3. Model-family-specific migration strength α values have been configured as described in Section 4/5.1: α=0.5 for OPT and BLOOM models, α=0.75 for GLM-130B (due to ~30% activation outliers), and other model-specific α values reported in Table 6/Table 7 (e.g., 0.8 for LLaMA, 0.85-0.9 for Llama-2, 0.6-0.7 for Falcon, 0.8 for Mistral/Mixtral).

The migration strength α has been set to 0.5 for all OPT and BLOOM models, as stated in Section 4 and Section 5.1: 'α = 0.5 is a well-balanced point to evenly split the quantization difficulty, especially when we are using the same quantizer for weights and activations (e.g., per-tensor, static quantization)' and 'The migration strength α = 0.5 is a general sweet spot for all the OPT and BLOOM models'.

The migration strength α has been set to 0.75 for GLM-130B, as stated in Section 4 and Section 5.1, because 'GLM-130B has ~30% outliers, which are more difficult for activation quantization', requiring a larger α to migrate more quantization difficulty to the weights than the default 0.5 used for OPT/BLOOM.
